en: After Chan Master Yue-lin passed away at Mount Wu-hui in Wukang, his disciple De-xiu, who followed the lineage of Yue, compiled a volume of his recorded sayings and requested me to write a preface.
I said: "This old man, amidst the state of non-discrimination, forcibly gave rise to discrimination."
Furthermore, one might wish to pursue and record this. Why? The two sons replied: "The Way does not belong to speech, nor does it belong to silence.

Both speech and silence fall into extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). If a student truly understands what is meant by 'speaking all day long yet never speaking,' then the composition of this record serves to untangle adhesions and loosen bonds; it would not be said to be without benefit. Otherwise, [it is like] *tīta*..."
The supreme flavor of ghee can, conversely, turn into a poisonous drug; how could one not find it strange that the Master [acted thus]?

As for me, I have shut myself away in a secluded place, contemplating those who are beyond the mundane world and with whom I share a bond of unyielding harmony—those like Yue Lin (Moon Forest) are truly hard to find. That my two sons were further able to understand the Master’s intent in this way is no small matter.
I have briefly recorded this to console his diligence and to relieve my own longing. The Chan Master’s name is Siguan; his dharma name is Yuelin.
He is the seventh generation in the direct lineage of Yangqi. Written on the first day of the Lantern Festival in the Wuyin year of the Jiading era by Chen Guiqian Yiwen of Sanyan.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Yue-lin.
Compiled by Attendant Fa-bao, these are the recorded sayings of Master Yue-lin while residing at Shengyin Chan Monastery in Li-kou, Pingjiang Prefecture.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jiatai era, the Master entered the monastery. Pointing to the triple gate, he said:
"The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; having no gate is the Dharma-gate. To enter the body-whole here is to find another heaven and earth."
Pointing to the Buddha hall, he said: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—all are marks. How can you explain the principle of what is 'non-mark'?
For now, we must simply share the incense and lamps; do not listen to the slander of bystanders."
According to the Abbot’s account: "He cuts off the vital ford and fully upholds the orthodox command; even if Buddhas and Patriarchs were to arrive, they would have to beg for their lives.
When the monk Chengtian Tong’an received the robe from the Master, the Master raised it and said: "At the head of Dayu Ridge, it could not be lifted;
Tong’an received it with his own hands and brought it here. Carelessly draped over the shoulder, it causes both ordinary people and sages to open their eyes wide."
Holding up the notice, he said: "At Vulture Peak, the entrustment was made with a great causal connection. When cast upon the ground, it made a golden sound; I now clearly present it for you to see.

Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "Dharma after dharma is not concealed; from ancient times to the present, it has been revealed in full majesty. Take this one step further, and I shall clearly proclaim it for you."
Ascending the seat, he held up the incense and said:

"This one portion of incense is respectfully offered to the present Emperor to pray for his sacred longevity—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years. Next, he held up incense again, saying:

"It is offered on behalf of the Governor, the Great Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and all the officials of the prefecture, to augment their venerable lifespans. Again, he held up incense and said: "This one..."

"A single incense offering. Do you know where it falls? Without being hidden away in a pouch, I burn it within the burner, to honor the late Great Monk, the Elder Abbot of Da Hong Mountain in Suizhou, in order to repay the kindness of his Dharma-milk.

Let it freely perfume the heavens and scorch the earth. Thereupon, he adjusted his robes, took his seat, and said: "The jeweled temple upon the tip of a hair; the wisdom-sword shines with brilliance."
A follower of the Chan school requested an audience. A monk asked, "I have heard your teaching that if one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Is this truly so, or not? The Master said, "It is not truly so. The monk asked, "Why is it not truly so?"
The Master said, "It is because you do not believe. The monk said, "Splitting open the face-gate, ugliness and clumsiness are exposed; it turns out the bearded man has no whiskers.

The Master said, "Watch the head-word (hua-tou). The monk said, "As for Chan Master Fayan’s saying, 'If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one does not see the Tathāgata,' I wonder what this means? The Master said, "There is an echo within the words. The monk—
[The monk] said: "When not a single thought arises, the whole body is manifest; as soon as the six sense organs stir, they are obscured by clouds.

The Master said: "You have hit the mark. The monk asked: "Regarding Sanxing’s saying, 'Whenever I meet someone, I come forth; but when I come forth, I do not act for others'—what is the meaning of this?"
The Master said, "Wrong. The monk asked, "Xinghua said, 'When I meet people, I do not come out; when I come out, I am for the sake of others. What about that? The Master said, "Wrong.
The monk said, "Xinghua’s spear and banner stand upright; Sansheng’s liver and gall are laid bare together."
The Master said, "He cannot be led. The monk asked, "How does the newly installed Abbot of Shengyin benefit people right now? The Master said, "One blow, one mark.
The monk said, "In emulating the ancients, he girds his waist with three strips of bamboo; in engaging with beings, he relies solely on a single fingertip.
The Master said, "You have wrongly applied these names and phrases. The monk bowed, and the Master let out a long sigh.
The Master then said: "All dharmas are empty as the seat; dwelling here, I preach the Dharma. Dharma after dharma is not concealed;
a pure breeze arises throughout the six realms. One step higher than the last, one stride wider than the last.
The old Gautama of the Yellow Face and this Dharma that came from the West—both have met with a total defeat right here. I dare ask the assembly: where is he?"
Regarding the point where he fell into error: "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon it long ago; even until now, he has not attained the wondrous.

Again, it is said: One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. When the great assembly had gathered and settled, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said, "The World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma is finished.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. Does the assembly still know the point where the ancient sage fell? "When the string is moved, the melody changes."
Leaves falling, one knows autumn has come; wind arises across the vast fields; waters flow toward the east.
On that evening, he gave a small *chan* (meditation) discourse, saying: "This ancient monastery of Shengyin is utterly serene by the lake. Who knows how many hundreds of years have passed?"

He already belongs to such a person. Even the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the western continent of Aparagoyānī, the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru are placed within the palm of his hand;
he casts the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters. Furthermore, how is this so? [The Master] claps his knee and says:
"The entire splendor of the world has been purchased at once, without spending a single coin."
The story is recounted again. Master Zhigong sent someone to deliver a message to Dharma Master Sida: "Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings?
What is the point of looking up at the Milky Way all the time? Sida replied, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have been swallowed by me in a single gulp;
where else could there be any sentient beings to be saved? The Master said, "Do you wish to recognize Sida? I pity the poor man..."
The Master, having ascended the hall, said: "The sun may grow cold; the moon may grow hot. No demons can destroy the True Teaching. But tell me, what is the True Teaching?
Ten words, nine of which hit the mark, are not as good as one moment of silence."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The ancient mirror is one zhang wide; empty space is one zhang wide. Holding up his whisk, he said:
'This [whisk] is within empty space, or outside empty space? Examine this!'"
Ascending the hall: It has been ten days since the summer retreat began. As for this matter—how is it? "When there is no wind, the lotus leaf moves;
there must be a fish swimming beneath. Ascending the hall: Every day is a good day; every moment is a good time. Why is this so? Because everyone [seeks it] at their own heels.
Below, one stumbles and misses the mark; it is precisely because things are so extremely clear that what is attained is made all the more delayed.
When Master Guangdu ascended the hall for formal instruction, he truly brought forth the teaching: "Before the Dharma Hall, the grass is a fathom deep.
He possessed such a strategic approach and such a model. Who is this? It is Master Guangdu, who strikes with his whisk.
The meditation seat. Descending from the seat.
Entering the hall. [The Master] cited a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. The Master said:
In ending human life, no further blade need be exerted; the four seas become one family, the winds calm and the waves stilled.
Upon ascending the seat for the Great Xiang (first anniversary) of Empress Ciyi: this world does not move, nor does that world change;
there is but a single firm and dense body, manifesting within all dust and atoms.
Ascending the hall: Today is the first day of the tenth month; it is on this very day that the furnace is opened. Zhaozhou’s dialogue regarding guest and host was brought forth by Shengyin.
It has been brought forth, and it has been brought forth; it has been explained, and it has been explained. But in the end, what is it? Return to the hall and go toward the fire.
Receiving the late Master Lih’s final letter, [Zhaozhou] ascended the hall and said: "Going, going—yet truly not going; coming, coming—yet truly not coming.
Coming and going are like dreams and illusions; in empty space, not a speck of dust remains. At this very moment, where is Master Tong’an? Raising his whisk, he said:
"He cannot remain within the rank of Buddhas and Patriarchs; last night, as always, he stayed among the reeds."

Ascending the hall. On the fifth day, ascending the hall. Morning after morning, entering the room; on the third and eighth days, the recitation of mantras—these are the regulations of the monastic groves.
He lets out a shout and says: "Delicious food is not for the satiated to eat."

Ascending the hall: Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires resolution this very day. "Resolution, resolution, resolution, resolution"—looking south, one gazes at the Big Dipper.
*Duḥ!* Ascending the hall: When hot, seek coolness; when cold, turn toward the fire; when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. Do not take...
The Record of Sayings from the Wushih Assembly at Chengtian Nengren Chan Monastery in Pingjiang Prefecture,
compiled by Attendant Faxu.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Samādhi of the World-Honored One was not known by Kāśyapa; the Samādhi of Kāśyapa was not known by Ānanda; the Samādhi of Ānanda was not known by Śāṇakavāsin.
From the patriarchs down through all the sages, their samādhis were mutually unknown. I dare ask you all: tell me, what is it that they do not know?
If you are of the swift and eminent class, you will immediately know where the point lies; otherwise, [you remain lost]."
"However, do not let your casual intellectual understanding bury the mind of the Patriarch.
He ascended the hall and raised the case of Venerable Piṇḍola: When King Aśoka asked him, "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha;
is this true? the Venerable One raised his eyebrows with his hand, remained silent for a long while, and then asked, "Do you understand? The King said, "I do not understand."
The Venerable One said, "The Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta once invited the Buddha for a meal; at that time, I was also included among his retinue.
The Master said, "Today, this great donor has entered the mountains to make offerings to the Arhats. I, this mountain monk, shall celebrate this feast by providing a commentary.
He raised his eyebrows with his hand and said, "Not recognized by the thousand sages from of old; the assembly on Mount Grdhrakuta remains as it was."
Nevertheless, it has been said for many days now. Entering the hall:
I have a turning phrase that has remained thus throughout kalpas; it is utterly remote, beyond the reach of people. "Gathered heads raise it together.
Since there is no one, who is raising it together? [He] cried out in a loud voice: "A lacquer bucket!"
Ascending the hall on the first day of the year: Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and the world is governed;
the patch-robed monk attains the One and his eyes are askance and his nose is straight. The imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace are both repaid at this one time.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Filling the eyes, it cannot be seen; filling the ears, it cannot be heard. This matter prior to the empty kalpa—I shall clearly present it to you.
You must take note of this: when meeting people, do not misrepresent it."
The Buddha ascends the hall for the occasion of his *parinirvāṇa*. "At this place, all Buddhas turn the Great Wheel of Dharma; at this place, all Buddhas enter *parinirvāṇa*.
At such a time as this, where can one see Old Śākyamuni? After a long silence, he said: "With palms joined at the triple gate."
Incense was burning in the Buddha Hall.
He ascended the hall and said: "In the lands of the ten directions, there is no realm where he does not manifest his body. Look up toward the heavens; who among you is one of those within?"

On the eighth day of the fourth month, ascending the hall, he surveyed the four quarters, pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, wielding the single point of focus alone. There was neither right nor wrong;
he universally requested that foul water be poured over his head, yet he did not forget the personal prediction he received at Vulture Peak.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ability to understand speech does not concern the tongue; the capacity to speak is not the sound itself.
In every land and within every atom, it is thus—where can one find a place to lodge one's whole body? He held up his staff and said, "Look, look! The staff has already met you all.
With a thump, he struck the ground and descended from the seat.
Xie Dian addressed the assembly from the seat, saying: "The monastic communities and Dharma circles have together achieved this. In years past, the Elder Xue employed this very device:
a handkerchief around his neck and a ladle at his waist; to this day, for a thousand ages, it remains a model of dignified conduct."

On the anniversary of the late Elder Abbot’s passing, he held up the incense and said: "Tsk! This venerable one—sweet in speech but bitter at heart—has brought us all to ruin, leaving our homes and households in disarray.
At this point where the monk has fallen into error, I shall state it directly and clearly: A single stick of sandalwood incense fills the universe;
who would say that gold is like mere dross?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment. At midnight, he beheld the morning star;
from this moment, thorns began to grow. Once these thorns grew, they were mistakenly transmitted throughout the human and celestial realms."
Small Sermon on New Year’s Eve: The year passes and the new year comes; this is the business of every year. Days come and days go; each day is ever renewed.
The wooden man claps his hands and laughs aloud: "A single stroke of brilliance cannot be painted. If you see it, see it—do not remain in dullness!
Above the tower, the horn of the new year has already been blown; before the hall, the lamp of the old year still flickers.

Again, he raised this case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is it like when the year has ended and the age is exhausted? The worthy said, "The old Wang of East Village burns paper money at night.
The Master said: "When the year has ended and the age is exhausted, what words are there? 'The old Wang of East Village burns paper money at night. Wild ghosts and idle spirits all hide their traces;
without dependence and without desire, one is a Golden Immortal."
Ascending the hall, he said: "This assembly has no branches or leaves; there are only those who are sincere and substantial. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.
Five thousand people withdrew from their seats. Raising his whisk, he said, "Look, look! The matter upon the edge of a sword is no trivial affair. He threw down the whisk and descended from the seat.
Proceeding to Wanshou to request the ascent of the hall, suddenly a clap of thunder rolls across the level ground. It startles the *jiaoming* insect so that its eyes open wide.
Neither saint nor commoner is established; what need is there to hinder dancing the *santai* wherever one may be?
Recorded by Attendant Qinghui for the *Lecture Record* of the Chan Master at Wanshou Baoen Guangxiao Chansi in Pingjiang Prefecture. Opening the Hall:
Holding his staff horizontally across his chest, he said: "Since you have come as the 'grass for Bodhidharma,' you must recognize this very thing. If...
If you recognize this very thing, I allow you all a place of practical application throughout the twelve hours of the day.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time were like this; the patriarchs of successive generations were like this; and the old monks of the world were like this.
Yet alone, Wanshou was not like this. Why? Because the old monk laughs and points toward the place where the monkeys cry—there is yet more spiritual efficacy.
His traces remain above. He throws down his staff and descends from the seat.

Entering the hall, there is no dharma that can be spoken; this is called preaching the Dharma. Upon a heap of refuse, he adds more refuse; turning it over completely to the bottom, he returns home and sits securely.
But tell me, how is it after arriving home? After a long silence, he said: "Above all, avoid the alms bowl."
Peace. He ascends the hall and says:
"One, two, three, four, five; five, four, three, two, one. The gates of immeasurable wondrous meanings all emerge from this sutra.
But tell me, from where does this sutra emerge? He strikes the meditation staff once and descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Qianfeng, who addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharmakāya has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance;
one must penetrate them all before one can sit securely. Yunmen stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Why does the person inside the hermitage not know what is happening outside?
Qianfeng laughed heartily. Yunmen said, "This is still where the student has doubts. Qianfeng said, "You..."
"What kind of mental activity is this? Yunmen said, "I must have the Master’s full confidence. Feng said, "You must act exactly like this before you can return home and sit in peace.
Yunmen responded with two "Nohos" and returned to the assembly. The Master said, "Ganfeng’s eyes were empty of the four seas; he was much like one who ignores everyone around him.
Yunmen was a connoisseur of the refined, yet he did not realize his tongue was trailing on the ground. At such a moment—"
Where could one look for these two great elders? A single drop of ink and water forms two dragons.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: “Zhaozhou has no Buddha-nature; Fenggan is far too talkative. Nanquan’s ‘a blade of grass’;
Yunmen’s ‘dry dung. And what about Wanshou? My mouth is full of tongues, yet none can speak it.”
Ascending the hall, he said: "How swift is the passage of time! It is like a white colt passing through a crack. Only for the patch-robed monks is every day a good day.
But ultimately, what excellence do these patch-robed monks possess? After a long silence, he said: "A thousand emptinesses do not equal one reality."
Ascending the hall: Last year’s plum, this year’s willow—its fragrance and color remain as they were. Not belonging to yin or yang, it is a spring of its own kind;
the numinous root has always been within our own house.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests a thousand, ten thousand, even a hundred billion bodies. From time to time he reveals himself to those of this age, yet the people of this age all fail to recognize him.
Now tell me, what is the face of one who does not recognize him? He struck a circular mark with his whisk and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the fourth month, he looked toward the four quarters and said: "The King of Dharmas—how shall one repay his virtue? Ascending the hall with a ladle of fragrant water, he said:
"A green spot upon the lips like a leopard’s mark; the tip of the tongue strikes true like a drum in the capital. A pair of mandarin ducks embroidered out."
"Look from the perspective of the Master: he does not hand the golden needle over to others. [He] throws down his whisk and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he cites Panshan: "The moon of mind is solitary and full; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects have vanished, what is it? [He] throws down his whisk and says: "It comes straight down—act quickly!"
Look! Entering the hall: The heat has receded and coolness arises; the wind is high and the dew is cold. Leaves fall and return to the root; heads are hidden and shadows are revealed.
Zhaozhou’s “tea” and Yunmen’s “millet cake”—what is the Way? Even those with clear eyes fall into the well. *Chan*.
Recorded by the attendant Faqing at the Chongxiao Xianqin Chan Temple in Lin’an Prefecture. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty; it was like buying a hat to fit a head. This year’s poverty is the true poverty; it is according to reality."
The case is closed. Last year I was so poor that I had no place even for a single awl; yet a thousand mouths still seemed too few.
This year I am so poor that I have not even an awl; yet a single body still seems too many. At such a time as this, what is to be done?
Who knows this meaning? It makes me remember Nanquan.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Vigilant and tranquil—this is it. Tranquil and vigilant—this is not. Abandoning the sweet peach tree, one climbs the mountain to pluck sour pears.
If you can understand within these words, let people compete to seek out the profound and subtle."
Ascending the hall: The midsummer heat blazes like a mass of fire; yet within it, there is naturally a place of coolness.
The rhinoceros fan is followed in vain; its towering horns—whom would dare to look upon them? If you look, how will you fare? A hawk flies off to Silla!
Ascending the hall: Time does not wait for man; the moon does not break the fifth day. As for that one point, I do not yet dare grant my approval.
Ascending the hall: [The Master] raised an example: There was once an old woman at Mount Tiantai. Whenever a monk asked, "Where does the road to Mount Tiantai go?
the woman would say, "Go straight ahead. As soon as the monk had walked three or five paces, the woman would say, "What a fine monk, yet you go like this!"
When Zhaozhou heard of this, he said, "Wait until I have examined her for you. Zhaozhou went there and questioned her as before; the old woman answered him as she had before.
Upon returning, Zhaozhou said to the assembly, "The old woman of Mount Tai—I have already examined and exposed her.
The Master said, "Go straight on! Go straight on! Under the clear blue sky and bright sun, she has been exposed. Not worth a single coin."
The Record of the Founding Patriarch of Baoyin Youci Chan Temple in Huzhou, compiled by Attendant Youzong. Upon entering the temple, he pointed to the Triple Gate and said:
"The pond is dug but does not wait for the moon; once the pond is complete, the moon comes of its own accord. When Hanshan meets Shishou..."
He attained it. Clapping his hands, he laughed heartily.

He ascended the seat; after the incense had been offered, the Master just then adjusted his robes and took his place. A monk immediately stepped forth from the assembly and said, "The field for selecting the Buddha has opened."
Having a doubt, he asked immediately. The Master said, "Wait three *ke*. The monk rose from his prostrations and said, "Please answer me right now.
The Master said, "You have already missed it. The monk said, "To seize the tiger’s head and catch the tiger’s tail—to clarify the fundamental principle within the very first phrase.
The Master said, "Torn asunder! The monk gave a shout; the Master also shouted. The monk asked, "Which phrase is this? The Master said, "I thought..."

The monk said, “The Buddha-eye is complete. The Master said, “A monk asked, ‘Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the sovereign attains the One and the empire is well-governed.
The Minister of State, seated here, attains the One and brings peace to the nation and security to the people. But when the Master attains the One, what then?
The Master replied, ‘Holding the Mohe sword crosswise, I issue the true command. The monk said, ‘I recall Wang Xizhi [Wang Youjun] giving up his seal as...’”
[The Master] said, "The temple has been the ancestral source for all under heaven. Today, you, Excellency, have newly constructed this Buddhist monastery and invited the Master to open the mountain.
Are these two cases the same or different? The Master said, "The orchid in spring and the chrysanthemum in autumn each possess their own fragrance.

The monk said, "When one has spirit, one adds to that spirit; where there is no elegance, there is still elegance. The Master said, "No dots need be added to the text. The monk said, "The subsequent text is long."
[The document] was entrusted for the following day. The Master said, "I wish to witness this grand achievement.
The Master then said, "His virtue accords with Heaven and Earth; his fame equals the sun and moon. Most honored and most noble, singular and refined.
The Tathāgata realized this and called it 'Unsurpassed Wisdom'; the Perfected One attained this and was titled the 'Unsurpassed Honored One. Truly, Heaven bestowed upon him jade."
The dew; golden lotuses spring up from the earth. Glorious and manifest before the sun, cutting off the ten directions—how do you speak this one phrase?
"When the waves of the four seas are stilled, the dragon sleeps soundly; when the clouds of the nine heavens are clear, the crane flies high. (The words of thanks are not recorded.)
Again, he raised the case: When the World-Honored One was on the path to enlightenment, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers as an offering to Dīpaṃkara.
Dīpaṃkara pointed to the place where the hair had been spread and said, "At this spot, a Brahma-shrine (Buddhist temple) should be established.

At that time, the Elder Sumati took a blade of grass, stuck it into the indicated spot, and said, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is complete. The Master said: "By planting a single blade of grass, the Brahma-shrine was newly renovated by Dīpaṃkara and the Elder."
This is already distressing enough. But tell me: what is the matter right now? Casually sitting and cutting off Jinchefeng Peak, the hundred rivers flow backward with a tumultuous roar.
Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: On the day the Tathāgata established the retreat, all conditions were suddenly stilled.
During this ninety-day long term, the patch-robed monks hang their mouths upon the wall. *Tu!* This is precisely the black ox lying in stagnant water.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Yangqi, who addressed the assembly, saying: "When body and mind are pure, all objects are pure; when all objects are pure, body and mind are pure.
Do you know where the old man Yangqi has landed? A fish bought on the boat is especially delicious."
"Having bought wine while treading through the snow, it is doubly fragrant.
He ascends the hall and says: "The warm breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool within. If you wish to know the ultimate meaning, I shall proclaim it with my staff.
He hurls down his staff and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Today is the auspicious festival of the First Full Moon. Throughout the earth and across the heavens, the stars and constellations emerge.
You should look with the eye of discernment before the pivot of action; do not let it slip past the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: A monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu replied, "This very mind is the Buddha.
The Master said, "If you can see it directly right now, then all the Buddhas of the three periods of time have manifested within this very place.
If this is not yet so, listen further to an ancient verse: 'Formless and shadowless, it penetrates the human breast; the peach blossoms of the second month are laid bare. Just..."
Plucking the yellow leaves from the trees, he enters the mountains and drives forth the white clouds.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Artifice comes to an end; my silence is infinite. Bodhidharma did not recognize this; his eyes were blind and his ears were deaf."
Recorded at Chongbao Chan Temple on Mount Lingyan in Pingjiang Prefecture;
compiled by Attendant Weigui. Ascending the hall:

Opening the eyes, one sees light; closing the eyes, one sees darkness. Whether opening or closing the eyes, to know this and yet deliberately transgress it—this is a single hair’s breadth [of delusion].
Heaven and earth appear upon his head. How laughable is Yunmen’s “Eh! and his looking at the mirror.
Entering the hall for a discourse, a monk asked: "The sun may grow cold and the moon may grow hot; no demons can destroy the True Teaching. I wonder, what is this True Teaching?
The Master said: "One blow leaves a mark; one slap draws blood. The monk said: "Just as it is..."
Master Baoning Yong said: "The tide rises to plant the rice, and the harvest yields a double crop; on the village road one meets people, half of whom are monks.
"Is this truly accurate? The Master replied, "It only accounts for eighty percent. The monk said, "If that is so, then today it is the Master [who speaks]."
[The monk] went beyond the realm of the ancients. The Master said, "Do not bury a fine person. The monk said, "I have heard that you, Master, once said:
'Nine out of ten words are hits; it is better than one silence. Does this truly constitute the authentic teaching?"

When insulted or reviled, he dissolved such things into the great void. With pack and hat, he wandered freely, following his nature toward the west or east.

When I first knew the Master, it was within the city of Helu; though we were separated for years, our meeting again brought us even closer. Now that I have come to visit, I find the Master afflicted by illness—his voice like the roll of thunder.

By day he roared like a lion; by night his physical form was cast off in silence. I know deeply that the Supreme Man is fundamentally without coming or going, yet why is it that I have not yet forgotten my bitter grief?

When the kalaviṅka has ceased its cry, the various birds fly about in confusion. Is it only the monastic community who remain deaf and blind? Is it that my Way is not right, that I have lost such a noble assistant?
Yet there remains a future affinity; I shall once more raise him up for the sake of the Master. He is a true son of the Jewel-fruit, one whom I have long cherished.
I hereby grant my seal of approval. A Dharma society shall be established at the valley of Longshan. Before long after the Master’s passing, I shall dwell together with him.
When offerings of pure food are laid before him, may he still testify to my words. May he enjoy this.
Epitaph for the Stupa of Chan Master Yue-lin Guan Composed by Chen Guiqian,
Grand Master of the Third Class with Audience Privileges, Administrator of Taiping Prefecture and its Military Affairs,
concurrently Managing Internal Observation, Agriculture, and Reclamation; and [recorded by] Shangfu Lang Chen Guiqian, Member of the Ministry of Rites.

Written by Lang Chen Yi for Zhao Shenfu, Grand Master of Court Petition (Chaoqing Dafu) and Vice Commissioner for the Survey and Transport of the Two Zhejiang Circuits (Zhen Baowen Ge Liangzhe Lu Jidu Zhuan Yun Fu Shi).
The master’s name was Guan; his Daoist style name was Yuelin. He was the son of Huang of Hougan, Fuzhou. At the age of eight, he tended cattle and held a whip.

In the midst of a scolding, he suddenly experienced a realization. He thereupon abstained from all pungent foods and meat. At the age of fourteen, he entered Xuefeng Mountain to seek out the practitioner Zhong and took ordination.
Soon after, he went to Ersheng Temple in Jingnan, where he devoted himself day and night to investigating the "Vzhou’s Dog" koan.

While washing a bowl, a verse spontaneously formed on his lips; from then on, his wisdom and understanding blossomed forth unexpectedly. The Master knew in his heart that this was not [the true state].

Without claiming any realization of the holy state, he shut his door and engaged in rigorous practice. (24) Having shaved his head and received the precepts, he dwelt on the mountain with full observance of the rites;
as for the standards of the precepts, he took [Master] Wei as his teacher. At that time, the elder monk Shi-Zheng was residing at Guangxiao Temple in Lizhou, where the Dharma was flourishing.
The Master went directly to his quarters. The Elder said, "If one can turn things around, one is identical to the Tathāgata. As for this incense altar before you—how do you turn it? The Master...
Yun said, "It strikes right where it hits. Nan shouted, "Go! When Nan withdrew from his seat, the Master traveled back and forth between Yungai and Guiyang for four years.
He then returned to Xuefeng and Gushan. At that time, Ke’an Ran and Youxi Yin were both in Min.
The Master traveled extensively, engaging with them in debate; yet, he considered himself still insufficiently realized.
Hearing that the venerable monk had moved to Jianfu Temple in Rao, he immediately followed him on foot. For another ten years, he studied the "Cloud Gate" (Yunmen) kōan regarding the "falling monk.
One day, while walking around the lotus pond, he raised the question himself: "Where is there the place where the monk fell? At this, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. Thereupon—
When he constructed the abbot’s quarters, Nanquan went there directly. Nanquan asked, "Where does the error lie? The Master said, "Is this not the speech of the scholar Zhang Zhuo?
Nanquan said, "Prostrate yourself. He then conferred the dharma robe upon him. From that time on, [the Master] fully attained the functional applications of the higher realm;
there were no longer any formidable fortresses before him. When Nanquan moved to Sijuzu and later to Dahong, the Master accompanied him on both occasions. Furthermore, he once visited...
In Luling, he met Changbuling (Never-Slight), who raised the koan, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha. The Master joined his palms in reverence.
Chang led the assembly and appointed the Master to the first seat. After a long time, he traveled east to Xuedou Mountain, where Zu’an Jian raised him up to establish him as a monk.
While traveling at Mount Yuyang, Foguang Zhaoguang asked the Master, "Does one who has attained awakening still have a self, or not?
The Master said, "I have already shown this to you, Zen Master. Zhaoguang said, "A lacquer bucket! The Master then gave a shout.

Recognizing that the Master was a true Dharma heir of an old monk, Zhaoguang asked, "Where did this monk's speech fall into error? The Master said, "Not a single stroke added to the text. Zhaoguang marveled all the more.
At that time, the Zen groves and Dharma caves all vied to have the Master as their preeminent leader. Changbuling resided at Ruiyan, and Tudu Ce resided at Shuangjing;
both extended invitations for the Master to share the teaching seat with them in verse. The Master consented to both. Tudu further presented a verse, saying:
"Having exhausted all the treasures of my life, I have by chance arrived at the summit of Mount Jing. Tudu smiles with a single [glance]."

When he spoke, only the other would nod his head in silent acknowledgment. Subsequently, he expounded the teachings for Dun’an, sharing the seat to preach on the "Section on Cultivation Without Realization.

Throughout the regions of Suzhou and Changzhou, both monastics and laypeople accorded him such high esteem that he could not remain hidden. By the beginning of the Jiatai era, he was already over fifty years of age.
The seat at Shengyin Temple in Wumen was vacant, and the various mountain monasteries joined in a formal request for the Master to assume its leadership.

He remained in meditative seclusion there for four years before being transferred to Chengtian Temple, and subsequently to Wanshou Temple. For many years, the people of Wu had long admired the Master’s spiritual conduct;

donors emptied their granaries to support him, and students seeking the Dharma kept his doorsteps constantly filled with visitors. This continued for nearly another decade until he grew weary of the constant demands of social engagement.

He retired to West Lake to plan for his final years. Li Kaifu (Liu Xiaoyou) established Bao-in Temple at Shangbai and, having prepared ceremonial robes and cap, went to the Master and earnestly requested that he serve as its founding patriarch (*kaishan*). Subsequently, he resided again at Lingyan in Pingjiang.
Later still, monks from Wu-hui Temple in Wukang, accompanied by several hundred local residents, circumambulated him in prostration and invited him once more.

He followed their exhortations with diligence. The place where he resided became a great monastic center (*mahāvihāra*). He extended compassion to all beings, employing skillful means (*upāya*) according to their respective capacities (*indriya*).
Yet, when he entered his quarters, his spiritual acuity was sharp and steep, leaving no room for intrusion. He sat upright day and night, his mindfulness penetrating through to the very marrow.

He occupied the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) six times; he carried nothing with him but a towel and an alms bowl (*pātra*), and if even the slightest thing did not accord with his principles, he would suddenly discard it.
He never looked back, and many people did not know where he was going. Wearing straw sandals and traveling on foot, he remained unchanged until old age.

At first, some may have suspected his conduct was born of affectation; however, as they followed him, many developed deep faith and became self-subdued through his influence. Indeed, such individuals were not few.

Later, he resided at Wuhui. At that time, he manifested illness; even when the drum struck twice for the midday meal, he would enter his room and say, "When the osmanthus flowers bloom, I shall depart.

He then ordered his disciples to prepare for the summer retreat in advance. Shortly thereafter, the osmanthus flowers indeed bloomed profusely. Rising early in the morning, he gathered the assembly for a general discourse.
He sat cross-legged in deep meditative absorption until the first watch of the night, when he looked at those around him and said, "The Old Śākyamuni was like this."
I was also like this. When my attendant monk requested that I leave behind a verse, I finished writing it, cast aside my brush, and departed.
This was the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the Dingchou year of the Jiading era. I had lived in the world for seventy-five years and sat in meditation for fifty-one summer retreats.

At my cremation, the smoke and mist coalesced into shapes like ceremonial canopies, and countless *śarīra* relics were produced, all of them manifesting in five colors. His disciples immediately erected a stupa on a western mound at the temple.

His bones were enshrined therein. His disciple Miaozhan succeeded him in residence at the mountain and truly venerated them. He came to my door and requested, saying, "My late master was long associated with you through friendship; moreover, he once sent me poems and composed a preface for his recorded sayings. Now I wish to obtain an inscription for him. The inscription reads: The mountain is high, the waters are deep, And the path to the peak is steep.

He who ascends it must exert himself; Only the steadfast can reach its summit. He who dwells here does not seek fame; He simply seeks to realize the Way. For thirty years he has lived in seclusion, Cultivating his mind in silent stillness. His virtue is like a hidden gem, His wisdom is as vast as the sky. He has long been a friend to the world, Yet remains detached from worldly affairs. His words are like a clear mirror, Reflecting the truth without distortion. Now that he has passed away, I write this to commemorate him. May his spirit rest in peace, And may his legacy endure forever.
Yangqi’s seventh generation, the lineage of Cold Clarity, manifests like the moon in water—appearing yet not being empty.
Having sat in six sites of enlightenment, he upheld the Patriarchal Command alone; like a great mass of fire, he melted the mundane and forged the holy.
Only Mount Wuhui is his teacher’s stupa; amidst green mountains and flowing springs, the wondrous Dharma is constantly preached.
Do not say that this stupa is sufficient to represent the Master; At midnight, there was a robe—may you be able to succeed to it.
The junior Dharma-disciple (De-xiu), respectfully praises this re-carving.

Chan Master Yue-lin Guan manifested in the human realm as the Immortal of Forbearance. He held aloft and wielded alone the Zen of the Patriarchs. Throughout his life, he carried but a single bowl with no fixed abode;
only his fame remains to be transmitted through the ages.
Having inherited the midnight robe of Xilin, he takes up his iron flute and blows it against the wind. With every falling word, he carries the entire burden;
that the green surpasses the blue is known only to himself.
With you, Master, we once shared karmic causes from past lives; a single smile spanned twenty springs at Wumen. Having met again, I have already forgotten the finger that points to the moon;
there are no words to praise the body of the Dharma King.
On the day of the Buddha’s Bathing Festival in the Dingchou year of the Jiading era, Chen Guiqian Yiwen of Sanyuan composed this text for Zen Master Yue-lin.
A veteran of the monastic community, his reputation spread in all directions; he presided over seven famous mountains, and both the ordained and the laity held him in deep reverence.
He bestowed words according to the capacity of his audience; his hand moved freely through square and round. Unrestrained by the lines and ink of convention, he cast aside all molds and ruts.

Truly, when he opened his mouth, it was not upon his tongue that one could find him. If you seek the standard within his words or pursue him on paper, you will be far, far removed from the moonlit grove.
Written on the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the tenth year of the Jiading era, the Year of Dingchou (1217), by Tiebian, residing at Chengtian Monastery in Pingjiang.
Postscript by Yuan Shao.
